1219.title: The little ones
1219.hook: Jesus warns fiercely against harming children (Matthew 18:6)
1219.howItsDone: Churches teach Jesus's care for children in Sunday school and preaching, and some congregations now train volunteers in child safeguarding, require background checks, and keep two adults with children at all times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, where churches disagree, and speaking the truth in love. Your line was love in disagreement.

The disciples are arguing about rank. They ask Jesus straight out: who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? Matthew says Jesus calls a little child over and sets the child in the middle of them. Just a small person standing in a circle of grown men who were, a minute ago, comparing themselves. Unless they become like this child, Jesus says, they won't enter the kingdom at all. Then comes a warning with no softness in it.

"But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea." A millstone was the heavy stone for grinding grain. Better, Jesus says, to sink than to do this. Offend, there, doesn't mean hurt someone's feelings. The Greek is about making someone stumble, setting a trap in their path. To cause a child to fall, in body or in faith, is what he warns against. A few verses later: "Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven." Children, in this picture, aren't small and forgettable. They have someone watching in the highest court there is. In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo parents and children away, Jesus is indignant: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Suffer there means allow. These words have a hard edge for churches today. Day one hundred forty-three named church hurt; here it reaches the youngest. Churches have had to face abuse within their own walls, and the failure to protect children. Some now answer with practical things: background checks, two adults in every room, clear ways to report, and listening to survivors. If a child is in danger, call local emergency help; if this stirs up something of your own, in the US you can call or text 988. Jesus didn't put the child at the edge of the circle. He put the child in the middle.

Bring to mind one child you're connected to, your own or someone else's, and picture them in the middle of the circle. Then ask a plain question: what would make them a little safer, a seat belt checked, an adult who listens, knowing who to call if something seems wrong? If you pray, you can pray for that child by name.
The little ones. Jesus's name for children, and for the small and trusting, set in the middle and fiercely protected in Matthew 18.
Your line: protect the little ones. In Matthew, their angels see the Father's face. Same time tomorrow.

1220.title: Yes means yes
1220.hook: truthfulness in all speech, not just under oath
1220.howItsDone: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians decline to swear oaths and make a solemn affirmation in court instead; other churches permit oaths for solemn occasions while teaching that all ordinary speech should be truthful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the little ones: a child set in the middle of the disciples, and a warning about millstones. Your line was protect the little ones.

"I swear, I'll be there at six." "Honestly, I loved it." "No, seriously, I'll pay you back." Listen to how much extra packaging people wrap around ordinary sentences to make them believable. As if a plain sentence, left on its own, might not be true. Jesus noticed the same habit in his own day, when people swore by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by their own heads, and quietly treated some oaths as more binding than others. His answer was short.

It's in the Sermon on the Mount. After telling his listeners not to swear at all, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." Notice what that does. If you need an oath to be believed, it suggests your ordinary words are a lower grade of truth. Swearing creates two kinds of speech: the sworn kind you must keep, and the everyday kind you can bend. Jesus folds them back into one. Every word is meant to be the sworn kind. James, writing to early Christians, repeats it almost word for word: "let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay." Christians have applied this in different ways. Quakers, Mennonites and some other churches take it literally and decline to swear oaths, even in court; they make a solemn affirmation instead. Other churches read Jesus as forbidding careless and manipulative oaths, not every oath. They point out that Paul calls God as his witness in his letters, and they allow oaths in court and at ordination. Both sides agree on the heart of it: a person whose plain word can be trusted without extra packaging. Yesterday's warning was about not making the little ones stumble. This one is about not making anyone guess. A yes that means yes. A no that means no. And no secret third option hidden behind the words.

Think of one thing you've said you would do that's still hanging, a call you promised, a favor, something you told a kid, and hold it plainly: no excuses, no reasons, just the yes you gave. Then notice how often your sentences reach for honestly or I swear, and whether they could stand on their own. If you pray, you can offer your words to God.
Yes means yes. Jesus's teaching in Matthew 5: let your yea be yea and your nay, nay, so that every plain word is as true as an oath.
Your line: plain truth. A plain yes, on its own, can be enough. See you soon.

1221.title: Tending the garden
1221.howItsDone: Christians practice creation care through church gardens, cleanups, energy and waste changes in congregations, and prayers for creation; some churches keep a Season of Creation each year, and Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant leaders have written on care for the earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yes means yes: Jesus folding oaths and ordinary speech into one kind of truth. Your line was plain truth.

A plastic bag snagged on a fence by the bus stop, flapping in the wind. Everybody walks past it. It isn't anybody's bag, so it isn't anybody's job. Now go back to the second chapter of the Bible. There's no city yet, no bus stop, no fence. There's a garden, and one human being, and before anything else goes wrong, God gives that human a job. Not a title. Not a throne. A job, with dirt under the fingernails.

Here's the verse, Genesis 2:15: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Two verbs. Readers of the Hebrew point out that the first is a word for working the ground that elsewhere also means to serve. The second, they note, means to keep, to guard, to watch over, and it's used for keeping God's commandments. So the human is placed in the garden as a gardener who serves it and a guard who protects it. Not an owner. A psalm makes the ownership plain: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Christians read the first chapter of Genesis too, where humans are given dominion over the creatures. Some readers once took dominion as permission to use things up. Others, reading it beside chapter two, hear dominion as the responsibility of a steward: ruling the way a good king rules, for the good of what's in his care. Francis of Assisi sang of Brother Sun and Sister Water. Leaders in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches have written about care for creation as part of faith, not a hobby beside it. It comes down to two old verbs: serve the ground, and guard it.

Picture a place you pass every day, a sidewalk, a parking lot, the hallway at work or school, and the bit of litter you always walk past there: a cup, a wrapper, a bag on a fence. Picture yourself bending down to pick it up, not as a big gesture, but as the job given in the garden. If you pray, you can give thanks for that small patch of earth.
Tending the garden. Creation care, from Genesis 2:15: the human placed in Eden to dress it and keep it, to serve the earth and guard it.
Your line: till and keep. A gardener and a guard, not an owner. Until tomorrow.

1222.title: The gold ring and the filthy coat
1222.hook: who gets the good seat? James, Jesus' guest list, and a love of preference for the poor
1222.carry: a preferential love for the poor
1222.howItsDone: Christians live this out through church food pantries, shelters and visiting ministries; Catholic social teaching names it the preferential option for the poor, and Methodist and other churches teach personal visiting alongside giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first job in Genesis: look after the ground. Your line was till and keep.

Two visitors come through the door of the meeting at the same moment. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes. The other wears a filthy coat. Someone hurries over to the first and says, in the old King James words, "Sit thou here in a good place." To the second: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." That scene is in the letter of James, and James asks his readers straight out whether they've started sorting people by their clothes. Underneath sits a plain question that any gathering answers, whether it means to or not: who gets the good seat?

Jesus answers the seat question at a dinner party in Luke's Gospel. Watching guests elbow toward the best places, he turns to the host with advice for next time: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind." And the reason: "for they cannot recompense thee." A guest list built on who can invite you back is a trade. A guest list that starts with the poor is a gift. Catholic teaching gives this a name, often called the preferential option for the poor; the Catholic catechism speaks of the poor as the object of the Church's preferential love. It doesn't mean God loves rich people less, or that being poor makes anyone holy. It means that when choices get made, about money, time, laws or who sits where, the needs of the poor are weighed first. Other churches arrive there by their own roads. John Wesley, the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement, preached a sermon on visiting the sick, pressing his hearers to go in person, not only to send help. Sending help is good, he said, but going yourself teaches what sending can't. You meet the people themselves: their faces, their names, what their week is actually like. So "first" turns out to be practical: the good seat, the top of the budget, and on an ordinary Tuesday, an hour given to someone who can't pay it back.

Bring to mind one person you know, or pass often, who is struggling to get by: a neighbor between jobs, a relative behind on rent, the man on the same corner every morning. Notice whether you know their name, and let them sit in the front row of your mind for a while, ahead of your own errands. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name, or by face if you don't know the name.
The poor first. When choices are made about money, time or a seat at the table, the needs of the poor are weighed before anyone else's.
Your line: a preferential love for the poor. First means the seat, the budget and your time. See you tomorrow.

1223.title: One blood, said in Athens
1223.hook: Paul in Athens: all nations made of one blood, so contempt for a race denies the image of God
1223.carry: one blood, every face God's image
1223.howItsDone: Christians teach this through the doctrine that every person bears the image of God; churches hold services and study groups on racial reconciliation, and some congregations deliberately bring together people of different races to worship side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold ring, a filthy coat, and one good seat. Your line was the poor first.

Paul is in Athens, and the city's thinkers have brought him up to the Areopagus to explain himself. He's been walking their streets, and he's found an altar with an inscription: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." So he starts there, with something of theirs. Then, partway through, he says a sentence that reaches far past that hill. God, he says, "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Not Athenians and then everyone else. Not one people as the original and the others as copies. One blood. Today, that sentence, and what it does to racism.

Paul's sentence stands on the first page of the Bible: "So God created man in his own image." Christians read that as true of every human face. Not some faces. Every one. Then Acts adds the family tree: one blood, all nations. Put the two together. If every person carries the image of God, and every nation shares one blood, then, in their reading, contempt for a race is contempt aimed at the image of God itself. That's why Christians who oppose racism call it a sin and not only bad manners. It denies something God made. Churches have not always lived this verse. Some Christians in history used the Bible to defend slavery and segregation. Other Christians, reading the same Bible, worked and suffered to end both, and they quoted lines like this one as they did. The verse didn't change. What changed was who was willing to hear it. Paul pushes it further in Galatians: "ye are all one in Christ Jesus." And in the last book of the Bible, John sees a vision of a great multitude "of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" standing before the throne. Notice what's still there at the end. Nations. Tongues. The differences aren't erased. Christians read this as oneness that isn't sameness: one family, every accent kept.

Bring to mind someone whose race or family story is different from yours: a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate, a voice you listen to. Ask yourself honestly what you've learned from them, and what you've never thought to ask; if a quick judgment about a whole group rises up, don't argue with it, just name it and set it down beside that one face. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person by name.
One blood. Paul's words in Athens: every nation shares one family, and every face carries the image of God.
Your line: one blood, every face God's image. Every nation, one family tree. I'll be here tomorrow.

1224.title: The stranger in your land
1224.hook: a law with a memory attached: love the stranger, for you were strangers (Leviticus 19:34)
1224.howItsDone: Christians practice this through church welcome teams, refugee and immigrant ministries, English classes and meals for newcomers, and through simple hospitality to new neighbors, often citing Leviticus 19:34 and Matthew 25:35.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul in Athens, beside an altar to the unknown god. Your line was one blood.

The first week somewhere new has its own small terrors. Which door is the real front door. Which line you're supposed to stand in. Whether that joke was friendly or not. Nobody tells you, and everyone else seems to know. Leviticus 19 is full of practical laws: pay your hired worker before morning, keep your scales honest. And near the end of it sits a law about exactly that person, the one who doesn't know where the front door is. It comes with a reason attached, and the reason is a memory.

This path met the stranger early, in Exodus, back on day three hundred ninety-six. The Hebrew word is ger: someone living among a people not their own, settled in, but not from here. The law about the ger in Leviticus 19 reads, in the King James Bible: "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Notice the words as thyself. They echo a line from earlier in the same chapter, love thy neighbor as thyself. The stranger gets the same love as the neighbor, not a lesser version. Then the reason. Not because strangers are useful, or because it's polite. Because you remember. Exodus says it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You know what it's like. Jewish neighbors read these laws first, as their own Torah, and Christians received them as scripture too. Jesus carries the thread further. In his picture of the last judgment in Matthew, the king says, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So, in this reading, the newcomer at the door may be closer to Christ than they look. Christians disagree, sincerely, about immigration laws and borders, and this path won't settle those arguments. But these texts speak to something smaller and harder: the actual person in front of you, who doesn't know where the front door is.

1225.title: Life and death questions
1225.hook: end-of-life care and the death penalty: Christians weigh them differently, all starting from the worth of each life
1225.howItsDone: Christians bring these questions to prayer, pastors, chaplains and church teaching; hospital chaplains sit with families making end-of-life decisions, and churches publish statements on end-of-life care and the death penalty that reach different conclusions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger, the newcomer who doesn't know where the front door is. Your line was love the stranger.

A woman sits in a hospital hallway with a form on her lap. Her father can't speak anymore, and the doctor has asked whether to keep every machine running. Across the city, in a courtroom, a jury is being asked a different question about a different life. For the people in those rooms, it isn't a debate on the news. Someone has to decide. This week has been asking who gets protected: children, the ground, the poor, every race, the stranger. Today it reaches the hardest edge of that: life and death questions.

Start with a line from the end of the Torah. Moses, in Deuteronomy, sets the choice in front of the people: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Christians on different sides of these debates can each appeal to that line; they disagree about what it asks. Take the end of life. The Catholic catechism, for one, draws a line. Stopping treatments that are only a burden, out of proportion to any good they can do, can be right: that's letting a dying person die in peace. Acting to end a life is something it rejects. Some other churches and individual Christians weigh assisted dying differently, and argue it out with care. Then the death penalty. Genesis 9 says, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man." Some Christians read the first half and hold that the state may take a murderer's life, pointing also to Paul's words that the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain." Others read the second half, the image of God, and say it's still there in the worst of us. The current Catholic catechism calls the death penalty inadmissible, and other Christians argue against it too. The answers differ. The starting point doesn't. Each side is arguing from the same root: each life is made by God, and matters to God.

Bring to mind one person facing a choice with no easy answer: a family deciding about care for someone they love, a friend at a crossroads. Keep them company in your mind, without deciding for them. If you pray, you can use a line from the Psalms, "My times are in thy hand"; if not, simply wish them wisdom and peace. If a decision like this is pressing on you, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Life and death questions. The hardest choices, where Christians reach different answers while starting from the same place: choose life, because each life matters to God.
Your line: every life counts. There's a life underneath every one of these arguments. Go gently.
